content: Uterine prolapse, also known as descensus uteri, refers to the downward displacement or sliding of the uterus from its normal anatomical position in the pelvic cavity into the vaginal canal. The uterus is typically supported by pelvic muscles, ligaments, and connective tissues. When these structures weaken, the uterus may descend into the vaginal canal. Risk Factors Uterine prolapse is more common in women who have experienced one or more vaginal deliveries. Aging and the reduction of estrogen levels after menopause can also contribute to the weakening of pelvic support structures, increasing the risk of prolapse. Chronic coughing and obesity exert additional pressure on the pelvic floor, further predisposing individuals to this condition. Although rare, pelvic tumors can also lead to uterine prolapse. Chronic constipation and the associated straining can exacerbate the condition. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Complications In severe cases of uterine prolapse, ulceration and infection of the cervix and vaginal walls may occur. A cystocele, or herniation of the bladder into the vaginal wall, can lead to urinary tract infections and other urinary symptoms. Similarly, a rectocele, or herniation of the rectum into the vaginal wall, may result in constipation and hemorrhoids. Prognosis Most women with mild uterine prolapse experience minimal or no bothersome symptoms and do not require treatment. Vaginal pessaries are an effective non-surgical option for many women. Surgical intervention often yields excellent outcomes, although some women may require additional treatment in the future. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Symptoms of uterine prolapse may include: A sensation of sitting on a small ball. Difficulty or pain during sexual intercourse. Frequent urination or an urgent need to empty the bladder. Low back pain. Pain during intercourse. Protrusion of the uterus and cervix through the vaginal opening. Recurrent bladder infections. A feeling of heaviness or pulling in the pelvis. Vaginal bleeding or increased vaginal discharge. Symptoms often worsen when standing or sitting for prolonged periods. Physical Examination A pelvic examination performed while the patient is bearing down (as if attempting to push out a baby) can reveal the extent of uterine descent: Mild prolapse: The cervix drops into the lower part of the vagina. Moderate prolapse: The cervix protrudes out of the vaginal opening. The examination may also identify associated conditions such as cystocele (bladder and anterior vaginal wall herniation) or rectocele (rectum and posterior vaginal wall herniation). The urethra and bladder may be positioned lower in the pelvis than normal. In rare cases, a pelvic mass may be detected if a tumor is causing the prolapse. Treatment Medical Therapy Treatment is not necessary unless symptoms are bothersome. Most women seek treatment when the uterus descends to the vaginal opening. Management options include vaginal pessaries or surgery. Vaginal Pessary A vaginal pessary is a rubber or plastic device, often donut-shaped, inserted into the vagina to support the uterus. It can be a temporary or permanent solution and is custom-fitted for each patient. Some pessaries resemble diaphragm devices used for contraception. Many women can be taught to insert, clean, and remove the pessary themselves. However, pessaries may cause irritation, abnormal-smelling discharge, or damage to the vaginal mucosa. They require periodic cleaning, sometimes performed by a healthcare provider. Certain pessaries may interfere with sexual intercourse by limiting penetration depth. Lifestyle Changes Weight loss is recommended for obese women with uterine prolapse. Avoiding heavy lifting and straining can help prevent symptom exacerbation. Chronic coughing should be managed, and smoking cessation is advised if the cough is related to smoking. Surgery Surgical intervention is considered when prolapse symptoms outweigh the risks of surgery. The choice of procedure depends on factors such as: The degree of prolapse. Desire for future pregnancies. Presence of other medical conditions. The patient’s preference to retain vaginal function. The patient’s age and overall health. Some surgical procedures, such as sacrospinous fixation, support the uterus using nearby ligaments without removing it. Other options include vaginal hysterectomy, which is often performed to correct uterine prolapse. Concurrently, any sagging of the vaginal walls, urethra, bladder, or rectum can be surgically addressed. Primary Prevention Strengthening the pelvic floor muscles through Kegel exercises can reduce the risk of uterine prolapse. In postmenopausal women, estrogen therapy (vaginal or oral) may help maintain connective tissue and muscle tone.
